topic: Introduction and History of Aviation Insurance
t: The world's first commercial passenger airline, DELAG, which operated Zeppelin airships in Germany, was founded in:
e: DELAG began airship passenger operations in 1909; scheduled fixed-wing airline services started in 1914 in Florida, USA.

topic: Introduction and History of Aviation Insurance
t: The repeal of the Air Corporations Act in 1994 was significant for Indian aviation insurance because it:
o: Made aviation insurance a tariff class
Allowed private scheduled airlines to operate, creating new fleets to be insured
e: Private carriers such as Jet Airways and later low-cost airlines entered after 1994, greatly expanding the aviation portfolio of Indian insurers.

t: Helicopters used for offshore and charter work in India generally operate at altitudes below about:
e: Helicopter operations are confined to the lower atmosphere (typically below 15,000 ft), exposing them to weather, obstacles and terrain hazards that are different from jet airliners.

t: Pilots are required to draw fuel samples from the aircraft tanks before flight mainly to check for:
e: Water condensation in tanks can cause engine stoppage; the pre-flight fuel drain is a standard operating procedure to detect water and sediment.

t: The nationality mark that appears in the registration of every Indian civil aircraft is:
e: Indian-registered aircraft carry the prefix VT followed by three letters (e.g. VT-ABC), allocated under the Aircraft Rules 1937.

t: The Chicago Convention has how many technical Annexes setting international standards and recommended practices (SARPs)?
e: There are 19 Annexes, Annex 19 (Safety Management) being the most recent; Annex 13 covers accident investigation and Annex 17 security.

t: The Warsaw Convention 1929 originally limited an air carrier's liability for death or injury of a passenger to:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Warsaw 1929 fixed the limit at 125,000 gold francs; the Hague Protocol 1955 doubled it to 250,000 francs, and the Montreal Agreement 1966 raised it to US $75,000 for flights touching the USA.

topic: Aviation Insurance Market and Classification of Risks
t: A broker places an airline risk and obtains written lines totalling 125%. An underwriter who wrote a 25% line will have a signed line of:
e: Lines are signed down proportionately: 25% × 100/125 = 20%.

topic: Aviation Insurance Market and Classification of Risks
t: The international trade body of airlines that develops standard conditions of carriage and dangerous goods regulations is:
e: IATA (founded 1945, headquartered in Montreal) is the airline association; ICAO is the UN agency, IUAI the insurers' union and AICG the clauses group.

t: The term 'Unit' in the hull breakdown exclusion of AVN 1C refers to:
o: A part or assembly of parts (including sub-assemblies) which has been assigned a time between overhaul or whose maintenance is tracked separately
e: The exclusion operates at Unit level: breakdown within a Unit and its consequences within that Unit are excluded, but resulting accidental damage to other Units is covered.

t: An aircraft with an agreed value of ₹60 crore is insured at an annual rate of 0.45%. The owner also buys hull war cover at 0.05%. The total annual hull premium (all-risks plus war) is:
e: All-risks: 0.45% × ₹60 crore = ₹27 lakh; war: 0.05% × ₹60 crore = ₹3 lakh; total ₹30 lakh.

t: A hull policy requires the aircraft to be operated in compliance with air navigation and airworthiness orders. A pilot flies with 12 passengers when the aircraft is certified for 9 seats and crashes. Insurers:
o: May decline the claim under the general exclusion regarding breach of airworthiness/operating regulations
Must pay because the overloading did not cause the crash
Must pay only the passenger liability
e: Carrying more passengers than certified breaches the C of A and regulations, bringing the general exclusions into play regardless of causation under the policy wording.

t: An airline's hull deductible policy carries an annual aggregate of ₹5 crore and reimburses each hull deductible of ₹1 crore. During the year the airline suffers seven partial losses each exceeding ₹1 crore. The hull deductible insurers pay in total:
e: Each deductible of ₹1 crore is reimbursed until the annual aggregate of ₹5 crore is exhausted; the remaining two deductibles fall on the airline.

t: An airline's liability for loss of checked baggage on an international flight under the Montreal Convention 1999 is:
o: Nil, as baggage is at owner's risk
Limited per passenger (originally 1,000 SDR, now revised upward) unless a special declaration of interest was made
e: Montreal fixes a per-passenger baggage limit (1,000 SDR originally, 1,288 SDR from 2019); the per-kilogram limit applies to cargo.

t: Under Montreal 1999, 200 kg of cargo is lost on an international flight. The carrier's liability (limit 22 SDR per kg) when 1 SDR = ₹110 and no special declaration was made is:
Which of the following is NOT a standard exclusion under Section II (third party) of AVN 1C?
o: Injury to a person on the ground struck by a wheel falling from the aircraft
Injury to employees of the insured
Damage to property owned by or in the custody of the insured
Injury to crew members while engaged in the operation of the aircraft
e: Injury to members of the public on the ground is exactly what Section II covers; employees, crew and the insured's own property are excluded.

t: A surplus treaty with a retention of ₹5 crore and nine lines gives the cedant automatic capacity of:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Capacity = retention + (lines × retention) = ₹5 crore + 9 × ₹5 crore = ₹50 crore; the treaty absorbs ₹45 crore above the retention.

t: An Indian airline is sued in India by the family of a passenger killed on a domestic flight. The applicable liability rules are:
o: The Warsaw Convention directly, as a treaty
The Carriage by Air Act 1972 as extended to domestic carriage by notification, applying Montreal-type rules
e: Conventions apply directly only to international carriage; India has applied the Convention rules to domestic flights through notifications under Section 8 of the 1972 Act.

t: The IATA Intercarrier Agreement on Passenger Liability (1995) was significant because participating airlines agreed to:
o: Waive the Warsaw liability limits for passenger death or injury
Insure passengers under personal accident policies
e: The Kuala Lumpur agreement voluntarily waived Warsaw limits and accepted strict liability up to 100,000 SDR, foreshadowing the Montreal Convention 1999.

t: AVN 48B contains paragraphs (a) to (g). Which of the following is covered by paragraph (g)?
o: Hijacking or any unlawful seizure or wrongful exercise of control of the aircraft
Any malicious act or act of sabotage
e: Paragraph (g) excludes hijacking; (a) war, (b) nuclear detonation, (c) strikes/riots, (d) political or terrorist acts, (e) malicious acts/sabotage, (f) confiscation.

t: Following a hostile detonation of a nuclear weapon anywhere in the world, under AVN 52E insurers may give notice of limited cancellation of war liability cover of:
e: AVN 52E provides 48 hours' limited cancellation after nuclear detonation or outbreak of war between the named powers, besides the normal 7 days' cancellation.

t: The clause AVN 72 inserted in London aviation policies excludes:
o: Rights of third parties under the UK Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999
e: AVN 72 prevents persons who are not party to the insurance contract from enforcing it under the 1999 UK Act, preserving the privity principle.

t: Which statement about the standard hull war policy LSW 555D is INCORRECT?
o: It can be cancelled by insurers on 7 days' notice
It covers confiscation by the government of registration of the aircraft
e: Confiscation by the state of registration is excluded, as insurers cannot cover an insured's own government seizing its aircraft.

t: Under AVN 1C Section V (Conditions), the insured is required to exercise due diligence and comply with air navigation regulations. This condition is important because:
o: Breach allows insurers to avoid liability for losses to which the breach contributed
e: The due diligence condition obliges the insured to maintain airworthiness and comply with regulations; insurers may rely on it where non-compliance contributes to a loss.

t: A Loss of Licence policy for a pilot with ATPL typically requires the pilot to hold a current DGCA medical certificate of:
e: Commercial and airline transport pilots must maintain a Class 1 medical; loss of this medical standard is the event insured.

t: A Loss of Licence policy with sum insured ₹1 crore provides that the lump-sum benefit reduces by 10% of the sum insured for each year of age beyond 50. A pilot aged 53 loses his licence permanently. The benefit payable is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Three years beyond 50 reduce the benefit by 30%, so ₹1 crore × 70% = ₹70 lakh; age-related reduction scales reflect the shortening remaining career.

t: An airport operator's liability policy generally EXCLUDES liability arising from:
o: Ownership, maintenance or use of aircraft by the airport operator itself
Operation of fire and rescue vehicles on the airfield
A baggage trolley striking a passenger
e: Aircraft operated by the airport are insured under aircraft hull/liability policies; the airport policy covers premises, operations, hangarkeeping and products.

t: A Products Liability policy for an aviation component manufacturer is usually written with:
o: Cover for the manufacturer's own faulty product
A per-occurrence limit and an annual aggregate limit
e: Products covers carry an aggregate because one defect can cause repeated losses; damage to the product itself is excluded.

t: Which of the following is a typical feature of a Personal Accident policy for aircrew?
o: Benefits are payable only if the licence is lost
Cover applies only on the ground
Benefits are a fixed scale (capital sums) for accidental death and permanent disablement, with flying risk specifically included
e: Ordinary PA policies often exclude flying other than as a passenger; crew PA specifically includes the flying risk and pays scheduled benefits.

t: Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (drones) in India are regulated by the Drone Rules 2021 issued under the Aircraft Act 1934. From an insurer's viewpoint, drone insurance mainly provides:
o: Loss of licence benefits for the remote pilot
Hull cover for the drone and third-party liability for injury or property damage caused by it
e: Drones carry no passengers; the exposures are physical loss of the unit and third-party liability, which insurers package as drone hull and liability policies.

t: An airline's hull programme earned premium of ₹50 crore last year and incurred claims of ₹65 crore. The loss ratio is:
e: Loss ratio = incurred claims ÷ earned premium = 65/50 = 130%, indicating an unprofitable account that will attract rate increases at renewal.

t: Which of the following documents would an aviation underwriter normally require before quoting on a general aviation aircraft?
o: Completed proposal form giving aircraft type, registration, value, use, pilots' experience and claims history
A list of passengers for the year
e: The proposal form (and often a copy of the C of A and pilot licences) gives the underwriter the information needed to rate hull and liability.

t: An airline with a poor loss record wants to reduce its hull premium. Which of the following would an underwriter most readily accept as a reason for a lower rate?
o: Reducing the agreed value below the lease requirement
Increasing the number of night flights
e: A higher deductible transfers small, frequent losses back to the airline and justifies a lower rate; reducing agreed value below finance requirements is not acceptable.

t: In rating airline hull risks, underwriters commonly compare the 'average fleet value' with the:
o: Maximum value of any one aircraft (the largest single exposure)
e: Average fleet value indicates the expected size of a total loss, while the maximum single value indicates the worst-case hull exposure and drives the insurer's line size.

t: Deduction for life insurance premium under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act is available up to an overall limit of:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹1,50,000 aggregate for all 80C items; premium qualifies only up to 10% of the sum assured for policies issued after 1 April 2012.

t: Under Article 20 of the Warsaw Convention 1929, the carrier is not liable if it proves that:
o: The passenger did not hold a valid passport
The accident occurred outside its home country
It and its agents had taken all necessary measures to avoid the damage, or that it was impossible to take such measures
e: Warsaw placed a rebuttable presumption of fault on the carrier; the 'all necessary measures' defence was removed by Montreal 1999 for claims within the first tier.

t: The Special Drawing Right (SDR) used in the Montreal Convention is:
o: A unit of account of the International Monetary Fund based on a basket of major currencies
e: The SDR's daily value is published by the IMF; Article 23 provides for conversion into national currency at the date of judgment.

t: Under the Warsaw Convention, a claimant may sue the carrier in any of the following jurisdictions EXCEPT:
o: The passenger's principal and permanent residence
The place where the contract was made
e: Warsaw Article 28 gave four fora: carrier's domicile, principal place of business, place of contract (where the ticket was bought) and destination; the passenger's residence became the fifth jurisdiction only under Montreal 1999.

t: The two conventions adopted at Montreal in 2009 deal with:
o: Compensation for damage caused by aircraft to third parties, under general risks and from unlawful interference
e: The 2009 General Risks Convention and Unlawful Interference Compensation Convention were intended to modernise the Rome 1952 regime for surface damage, but have attracted few ratifications.

t: The Hague Convention 1970 and the Montreal Convention 1971 respectively deal with:
o: Unlawful seizure (hijacking) of aircraft and unlawful acts against the safety of civil aviation (sabotage)
e: These security conventions oblige states to criminalise and prosecute or extradite hijackers and saboteurs, complementing the Tokyo Convention 1963.

t: The Schedules to the Carriage by Air Act 1972 (as amended) contain the texts of:
o: First Schedule: Chicago 1944; Second Schedule: Rome 1952
First Schedule: Warsaw 1929; Second Schedule: Warsaw as amended by Hague 1955; Third Schedule: Montreal 1999
e: The Act applies whichever text governs the particular carriage, depending on which instruments the states of departure and destination have ratified.

t: An aircraft hull claim arises from an accident. Which of the following would the insurers' surveyor be LEAST likely to examine?
o: Maintenance records and the C of A validity
Pilot licences and recency of experience
The passenger manifest to assess liability claims
e: Surveyors verify compliance with policy conditions (airworthiness, pilots), quantify damage and gather liability information; advertising spend is irrelevant.

t: Under the ICAO Annex 13 definition, damage to an aircraft limited to a single engine, propellers, wing tips, tyres or minor dents does NOT by itself make an occurrence an:
e: Annex 13 excludes such limited damage from 'accident' status because it does not adversely affect structural strength or flight characteristics.

t: In adjusting an aircraft partial loss, which of the following is normally recoverable in addition to the actual repair cost?
o: Loss of passenger revenue during repair
Depreciation in resale value after repair
Reasonable cost of transporting parts and the aircraft to the place of repair, and ferry flight costs
Cost of a replacement aircraft hired during repairs
e: The hull policy pays repair plus necessary transport and ferry costs; loss of use, diminution in value and hire of substitute aircraft are excluded consequential losses.

t: After a crash, an airline wants to make immediate payments to victims' families. Under its liability policy it should:
o: Pay and then claim from insurers regardless of policy terms
Wait for the court verdict before any payment
Obtain insurers' consent first, since advance payments are normally made with insurers' agreement and without admission of liability
e: Liability policies prohibit admissions or payments without consent; insurers routinely agree to advance payments under Montreal Article 28 while reserving liability.

t: Deduction for health insurance premium under Section 80D for an individual below 60 years (self and family) is up to:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹25,000; ₹50,000 where the insured is a senior citizen; an additional ₹25,000/₹50,000 for parents.

t: An aviation XL programme has two layers: ₹20 crore excess of ₹10 crore and ₹70 crore excess of ₹30 crore. A loss of ₹55 crore occurs. The second-layer reinsurer pays:
e: Cedant bears ₹10 crore, first layer pays ₹20 crore (up to ₹30 crore) and the second layer pays the excess above ₹30 crore, i.e. ₹25 crore.

t: The 'follow the fortunes' principle in proportional reinsurance means that the reinsurer:
o: Must accept any risk the cedant chooses
Shares the cedant's underwriting results and claim settlements made in good faith within the terms of the original policy
Can refuse claims it did not approve
e: Reinsurers are bound by the cedant's reasonable, good-faith settlements; this is distinct from claims control clauses that give reinsurers settlement rights.

t: A proportional aviation treaty pays the cedant a reinsurance commission of 20% on ceded premium. If ₹5 crore of premium is ceded, the commission is:
e: Commission reimburses the cedant for acquisition and administration costs: 20% of ₹5 crore = ₹1 crore.

t: 'Reinstatement' in an aviation excess of loss treaty refers to:
o: Restoring the cedant's licence after suspension
Restoring the layer limit after it is used by a loss, usually on payment of an additional premium
Returning premium when no loss occurs
e: XL treaties typically allow one or more reinstatements, with the reinstatement premium often pro rata to the amount of limit used.
